atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows.

This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer.

Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics.

contexts:
Add shared KMS client abstraction with explicit timeouts + standardized retries

Summary: Introduces a shared KMS client abstraction used across control-plane + data-plane services to standardize timeouts, retries/backoff, and error mapping. The current KMS call sites implement timeouts inconsistently (or not at all) and several retry policies amplify load during provider-side latency spikes, which contributed to elevated 5xx during throttling events.

Key goals: - Make KMS dependency behavior predictable (bounded latency, bounded retries) - Provide a canonical error taxonomy for downstream policy (circuit breaker + degrade-mode followups) - Improve observability: metrics + structured log fields to enable on-call triage

Scope of this PR: - New library package `pkg/kmsclient` with:   - explicit deadlines for Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/DescribeKey (per-operation defaults)   - retry policy w/ exponential backoff + jitter and a hard retry budget (max attempts and max elapsed)   - structured error mapping into a small set of categories (Timeout, Throttled, AccessDenied, NotFound, InvalidCiphertext, Internal, Unknown) - Minimal integration in two representative services to prove wiring + config surface (more migrations tracked in ENG-4823) - Adds unit tests for error mapping + retry budget behavior and a small fake KMS transport for deterministic tests

Non-goals: - Circuit breaker and degrade behavior (follow-up ENG-4824) - Metrics/tracing spans (follow-up PR; this keeps the wrapper API stable first) - Rotation / dual-read (ADR-008 work)

Configuration: - Defaults are conservative and aimed at production safety. Services can override via config, but values are validated and clamped to safe ranges in a later PR (ENG-4823 subtask). - Default budgets (v1):   - Encrypt/GenerateDataKey: timeout 2s, max attempts 3, max elapsed 3s   - Decrypt: timeout 2s, max attempts 2, max elapsed 2.5s (intentionally tighter to avoid fan-out storms) - Retryable errors: network timeouts, 5xx from provider SDK, explicit Throttling/RateExceeded

Error mapping: - Wrapper returns `KmsError` with fields: `category`, `provider_code`, `provider_message`, `is_retryable`, `request_id` (when available) - Logs should include: `kms.op`, `kms.category`, `kms.provider_code`, `kms.request_id`

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

## Required log fields
All logs emitted for KMS failures MUST include:
- `kms.provider`: `aws|gcp|azure|other`
- `kms.operation`: `Encrypt|Decrypt|GenerateDataKey|DescribeKey|GetPublicKey|...`
- `kms.key_id`: stable logical identifier (redacted if customer policy requires; see below)
- `kms.key_arn`: when available; may be redacted/hashed in Private (configurable)
- `kms.region`
- `kms.request_id`: provider request id if available
- `kms.error.kind`: one of the canonical taxonomy values above
- `kms.error.code`: raw provider code (e.g., `AccessDeniedException`, `ThrottlingException`)
- `kms.http_status`: when available
- `kms.retryable`: `true|false`
- `kms.retry.count`: retry attempts executed for this request
- `kms.latency_ms`: end-to-end wrapper latency

Optional but recommended:
- `kms.circuit_breaker.state`: `closed|open|half_open`
- `kms.timeout_budget_ms`: configured deadline for the operation
- `kms.throttle`: `true|false` (alias for filtering; derived from kind/code)
- `trace_id` / `span_id` (already standard, but called out here because dashboards depend on it)

Redaction guidance:
- Never log plaintext, decrypted payloads, or DEK material.
- `kms.key_arn` may be considered sensitive for some Private customers; if `KMS_LOG_KEY_ARNS=false`, log a stable hash in `kms.key_arn_hash` and omit `kms.key_arn`.

## Implementation details
Most changes live in the shared wrapper package (doc + constants), plus small call-site updates to align field names.

Example (Go) mapping and logging:

```go
// kmsx/errors.go
// KmsErrorKind is the canonical classification used for logs/metrics/alerts.
// See /docs/internal/kms-error-taxonomy.md.
type KmsErrorKind string

Document KMS error taxonomy in code and logs

## Summary
This PR adds inline documentation and concrete conventions for how we represent KMS failures in logs and traces. The goal is to make triage consistent across services (control plane + data plane) and to ensure dashboards/alerts can rely on stable field names.

This is intentionally “docs + conventions + guardrails”, not functional behavior changes. It complements the wrapper work in pr-18421 and metrics/spans work in pr-18434.

Linked: ENG-4822 (taxonomy + metrics tags), ENG-4823 (wrapper).

## What changed
- Adds a canonical KMS error taxonomy enum (with mapping notes) and documents when each category is used.
- Defines structured log field names + required fields for all KMS failures.
- Documents how errors should be surfaced to operators (what’s safe to include, what must be redacted).
- Adds a small helper that ensures required KMS log fields are present when logging wrapper errors (compile-time references + unit tests).

## Canonical taxonomy (required)
When a KMS operation fails, the wrapper MUST map to one of these kinds:
- `AccessDenied` (IAM/principal/key policy; includes `kms:Decrypt` denied)
- `NotFound` (key ARN/id not found, alias missing)
- `Throttling` (rate exceeded / quota)
- `Timeout` (client-side deadline, upstream hang)
- `InvalidCiphertext` (decrypt fails due to wrong key/material mismatch)
- `KeyDisabled` (key disabled/pending deletion)
- `DependencyUnavailable` (upstream service error/outage; retryable)
- `Unknown` (fallback bucket; should be rare and triggers follow-up)

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping (AWS-style error codes), retry budget accounting, and jitter range (non-deterministic aspects bounded via seeded RNG) - Adds a small integration-ish test using the fake transport to simulate throttle then success and assert we do not exceed max elapsed

Rollout plan: - Land wrapper, then migrate call sites incrementally behind a service-level config toggle where practical - SRE requested we ship metrics prior to broad rollout; follow-up PR will add `kms_client_latency_ms` histogram and `kms_client_errors_total` counter with tags

question: For the rollout of the new residency-proofing middleware and audit entropy hashing, what are the staged enablement steps, what should ops monitor, and what rollback action is available if key provisioning fails?
answer:
The staged enablement steps are:

1. Enable `feature.audit_entropy_hashing` in staging and run audit search regression.
2. Enable `feature.residency_proofs` behind a canary for 1% of requests with non-blocking enforcement.
3. Monitor SLOs and audit query latency.
4. Gradually increase the canary and enable enforcement.
5. Run the backfill migration for `seed_epoch` where requested by customer support.

Ops should monitor:
- SLOs
- Audit query latency
- Secrets store quota during onboarding, since provisioning creates per-tenant seeds

If key provisioning fails, the rollback action is to use the admin endpoint `/internal/flags/disable` to disable the feature, and run migration rollbacks.

Add residency-proofing middleware and audit entropy hashing

Motivation: Customers operating under strong data residency constraints need cryptographic proof that KMS operations and key usage occurred in the expected region without exposing deterministic audit identifiers that could be used to correlate requests across tenants. This PR introduces a residency-proofing middleware that records signed, region-anchored statements for KMS operations and an audit entropy-hashing layer that salts audit identifiers before logging to reduce cross-tenant correlation risk.

What this change does: Adds a lightweight middleware component in the frontdoor service that: (1) validates KMS provider region against tenant policy, (2) emits a residency proof blob signed by the platform's attestation key, and (3) attaches a short immutable nonce reference to the outgoing audit envelope. Introduces an audit hashing pipeline stage that applies HMAC-SHA256 with a per-tenant entropy seed (rotated periodically) to resource identifiers before they hit the audit log. Adds RBAC v2 enforcement rules that require the new residency-proof scope for operators who can override region pins. Feature-flagged rollout: residency-proofing is behind feature flag feature.residency_proofs and audit-hash behind feature.audit_entropy_hashing.

Risk and mitigation: New cryptographic material is added (attestation key and per-tenant entropy seeds). Keys are provisioned via the KMS provisioning flow and stored in the secrets store with restricted ACLs. CI includes integration tests that exercise seed rotation and residency proof verification. We ship a migration that backfills proof metadata where possible but does not change existing audit formats unless the feature flag is enabled.

question: What did that PR actually change to stop the SDK from being randomly unreliable during long-running live connections, and which SDKs were updated so they all work the same way now?
answer:
The PR changed three main things to reduce random unreliability during long-running streaming/live connections:

1. It explicitly propagates the server-issued session TTL to SDK session managers.
2. It adds an optional lightweight heartbeat/ping helper on streaming handles so ephemeral sessions can be kept alive without users managing their own timers.
3. It exposes a compact consumer-facing StreamFacade to simplify reconnect, backoff, and credential refresh.

It also harmonized retry/backoff and streaming helper behavior across SDKs by introducing a shared transport-agnostic `RetryProfile` and consistent stream helpers.

The SDKs updated so they behave consistently were:
- Python
- TypeScript
- Go

Associated version bumps mentioned were:
- Python SDK: 0.12.0
- TypeScript SDK: 1.27.0
- Go SDK: 1.8.0
contexts:
align-auth-ttl-heartbeat-and-stream-facade-across-sdks

Context & motivation: Multiple SDK consumers reported subtle mismatches between server-side session TTL propagation, streaming heartbeats, and SDK-side retry/keepalive semantics.

This caused short-lived production flakes where long-lived streaming clients were reauthorized unexpectedly or experienced silent stalls.

This PR harmonizes the contract across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs: 1) explicitly propagate server-issued session TTL to SDK session managers; 2) provide an optional lightweight heartbeat/ping helper on streaming handles to keep ephemeral sessions alive without user-managed timers; 3) expose a compact consumer-facing StreamFacade that simplifies reconnect + backoff + credential refresh for most application scenarios.

unify-retry-profiles-and-lightweight-stream-helpers-across-sdks

Motivation: SDKs historically contained duplicated retry/backoff and stream ergonomics code that diverged subtly between Python/TypeScript/Go. That made cross-SDK behavior inconsistent (different default jitter, different max_retry windows) and increased maintenance burden. This PR extracts a transport-agnostic RetryProfile and introduces a tiny, consistent set of lightweight stream helpers for each SDK so app code can be ported with fewer surface changes.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduce a core RetryProfile concept and backoff parameter mapping used by all SDKs (max_attempts, initial_backoff_ms, max_backoff_ms, jitter_mode, hedged_retries).
- Replace ad-hoc retry logic in each SDK with small adapters that map RetryProfile -> transport specific retry strategies.
- Add ergonomic streaming helpers: Python async generator wrapper (stream.iter_lines_safe), TS async iterable shim (stream.consumeSafe), Go StreamHandle interface + convenience ReadPump.
- Add cross-SDK unit/compat tests that assert parity on default retry timeline for common scenarios (auth 401 then refresh, transient 429, slow downstream).
- Documentation: migration guide and explicit examples for moving from the legacy per-SDK backoff flags to the unified RetryProfile.
- Version bumps: python sdk -> 0.12.0, typescript sdk -> 1.27.0, go sdk -> 1.8.0.

Why transport-agnostic RetryProfile: Teams run heterogeneous stacks (frontend TS, backend Python, microservice in Go). Previously, moving a workload between services required tuning three different knobs. The RetryProfile is a single well-documented primitive that can be serialized as JSON, stored in config, and applied consistently across languages.

Migration notes:
- If you set per-SDK backoff env flags (RETRY_INITIAL_MS, RETRY_MAX_MS, RETRY_ATTEMPTS), they will continue to be read but are deprecated — migrate to a RetryProfile config shipped to your service.
- Streaming helper names changed: start_stream -> open_stream is preserved at the transport level but helper names for safe iteration are new (see examples in docs/sdk/migration/retry-profile.md).

Scope and risk: The change is primarily additive (new adapters + helpers) but rewires retry decision points in each SDK. We validated with end-to-end test harness and Canary run against staging traffic for 48h.

Improve stream teardown, retry/backoff and reconnect semantics for OpenAI-compatible streaming

Fixes a class of customer-facing streaming failures observed when clients disconnect mid-stream and then reconnect or retry. This PR centralizes stream teardown logic, adds an explicit session idempotency token for resume/reconnect, implements server-side exponential backoff for automatic retry attempts, and updates the OpenAI-compatibility adapter to preserve in-flight function/tool-call state across reconnects. Key goals: 1) avoid duplicate function/tool calls on client reconnect, 2) ensure server timeouts produce a deterministic terminal event that client SDKs can use for cleanup, 3) make streaming retries safe under load without amplifying downstream work. This is implemented as a small runtime change plus adapter and SDK patches and includes unit+integration tests and a controlled rollout plan. Migration notes: server behavior is backward-compatible for clients that don't use resume tokens; SDKs should be updated to take advantage of resume and idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate tool calls. Unify session telemetry and introduce compact SDK adapter bridge

Summary: This PR introduces a compact adapter layer across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs that standardizes session telemetry envelopes, simplifies the streaming handoff surface, and provides a compatibility bridge so existing consumers can opt into the new ergonomics incrementally.

Motivation: Multiple internal integrations observed inconsistent session envelope shapes, duplicated telemetry keys, and slightly different retry defaults between SDKs leading to confusion for platform teams and noisy alerting.

This was called out in ENG-2143 and tracked as part of cross-SDK parity work in ENG-2199.

Goals: (1) standardize the session telemetry payload and sampling keys across SDKs; (2) provide a minimal adapter that consumers can layer over existing session code to get the new semantics with zero downtime; (3) align retry default presets for streaming and token refresh so cross-language clients have comparable behavior; (4) bump SDK minor versions that contain the ergonomic API surface.

Changes: - Core: new compact adapter module implemented in each SDK repo (redwood-sdk-python, redwood-sdk-typescript, redwood-sdk-go) and exported from the polyglot 'redwood' root package so examples can import a single compatibility shims path. - Telemetry: unified envelope format: {"session_id","span_id","sampling_rate","client_version","env_tags"} and a lightweight sampler hook.

Existing telemetry keys are preserved as aliases for backwards compatibility. - Streaming ergonomics: introduced 'CompactSession.handle' API that wraps existing pullstream/pushstream handles and provides a small set of methods (start, pause, drain, handoff) with clearer lifecycle semantics. - Retry presets: converged streaming retry presets to 'aggressive' (low-latency, limited retries), 'balanced' (default), and 'durable' (longer tail, idempotent workloads).

SDKs ship default 'balanced' to avoid changing runtime behavior for most users. - Version bumps: python -> 2.6.0, typescript -> 1.9.0, go -> 1.5.1. - Tests: added cross-sdk unit tests for envelope normalization and an interop smoke test that runs in CI job 'sdk-interop'.

heterogeneous-attention-fusion-with-staged-scheduler-and-continuous-batching-support

Motivation: reduce p99 latency regression for mixed-sequence workloads and improve throughput for production chat and retrieval runtimes by selecting optimal attention kernels at runtime and enabling continuous batching without sacrificing KV cache hit stability.

Changes: Introduces a heterogeneous attention selection layer (HeteroAttn) that picks between a low-latency microkernel and a high-throughput Flash-like kernel based on sequence length heuristics and current queueing pressure; adds a staged scheduler that enforces a short-term reservation window for latency-sensitive requests and a batch-aggregation window for throughput requests; implements a cooperative KV cache eviction policy (staged LRU) that works with continuous batching to avoid repeated cache thrash during rollups; adds fused rotary/rope offset precomputation paths that avoid memcpy for common rotary patterns; integrates fp16 accumulation path with optional fp32 fallback for edge-case stability; exposes runtime knobs: ATTEN_SELECT_WINDOW_MS, KV_STAGED_WINDOW, CBATCH_MAX_WAIT_MS for tuned rollouts.

Testing and validation: microbenchmarked on c6i-gpu clusters and internal perf-lab; added synthetic mixed-sequence workload harness and end-to-end chat replay traces.

Results: median latency improved 6-9% on mid-sized seqs, p99 reduced up to 22% for mixed workloads, throughput increased 12% on long-sequence tails while KV miss rate decreased 18% under continuous batching.

Rollout plan: staged canary on dedicated pool alpha -> 50% traffic after 72h, automatic rollback on p99 regressions >10% or error rate increase >0.5%.

Backwards compatibility: no API changes.

Known limitations: rare fp16 accumulation differences at extreme sequence lengths (documented and guarded by runtime flag), scheduler parameters tuned for our standard clusters; customers on small on-prem may require adjustments.

Hybrid signal-attn kernel with rotary-sparsity fusion and KV prefetch scheduler

Motivation: Production workloads exhibit mixed sequence length distributions and intermittent sparsity from rotary/rope quantization artifacts. Existing Flash-style kernels are high-throughput for dense attention but underutilize opportunities where token locality and structured sparsity exist. This PR introduces 'signal-attn', a hybrid kernel that combines a fast-path Flash-like matmul for dense regions and a lightweight sparse-merge engine for rotary-sparsity lanes. The kernel integrates with the serving runtime scheduler using a signal-driven prefetch heuristic for the KV cache and a continuous-batching hint that reduces tail latency without sacrificing throughput.

Summary: Implement a new attention kernel and scheduler hooks that: 1) Detect per-batch rotary-sparsity patterns (simple entropy+mask heuristics) and route attention work to either dense or hybrid execution path. 2) Fuse rotary/rope application into the QKV projection pipeline to avoid an extra transpose+allocate in the hot path. 3) Add KV prefetch scheduler hints that prioritize hot shards and stagger prefetch to avoid PCIe contention under bursty arrival patterns. 4) Expose a runtime config flag to tune the hybrid threshold and continuous-batcher latency budget.

Benchmarks: Microbenchmarks run on p4d-like instance (A100 style) with representative models: - 7B dense: 15% throughput increase, 12% median latency reduction, 9% p99 reduction. - 13B mixed-length: 22% throughput increase, 17% median latency reduction, 18% p99 reduction. - 70B semi-sparse eval (synth rope sparsity): 25% throughput uplift on best-effort routing, 23% p99 reduction after warm-up. End-to-end synthetic RLHF workload saw a 14% token-cost reduction due to fewer recomputations and better batching. Full benchmark logs attached in artifacts.
